title.narrative: Preventing Healthcare Associated Infection and Antimicrobial Resistance in Africa

description.narrative: To address Healthcare Associated Infection (HAI) in Africa, the project will use cutting edge molecular microbiology and mathematical modelling to investigate the implementation of the WHO framework for Infection Prevention and Control (IPC) in Malawi. Key to this will be the development of equitable partnerships with the Ministry of Health and the Kamuzu University of Health Sciences. The project will use the data to develop effective, acceptable and scalable interventions to reduce HAI in Africa. Background - Hospitals are complex environments that offer people care for diverse life events, from minor ailments to end-of-life care. They are perceived as places of safety, however the concentration of vulnerable people, staff and visitors makes maintaining safety a major challenge that requires the involvement of multiple professional groups and which requires the collective involvement of patients, staff and visitors. Infections contracted as a result of admission to hospital, or exposure to other healthcare facilities represent the most common adverse outcome associated with healthcare settings globally. Further, the germs, specifically bacteria, associated with HAI are increasingly resistant to antibiotics, making the treatment of HAI an increasing challenge. It is therefore best to prevent HAI happening in the first place. Infection prevention and control (IPC) is the term used to describe strategies to prevent HAI and the World Health Organisation has published a substantial body of work to support the implementation of IPC in low- and middle-income countries (LMIC). However HAI and IPC are often not prioritised in LMIC due to lack of resources and multiple competing priorities. Design and Methods - The project will work in three government hospitals in Malawi. The project will be based at the Malawi Liverpool Wellcome Programme and will run in partnership with the Kamuzu University of Health Sciences and the , Ministry of Health. There will be 4 workstrands: Implementing IPC strategy (Workstrand 1): The first priority will be to conduct formative research to design and develop appropriate strategies for the implementation of the WHO Core Components of Infection prevention. The team will investigate the success or failure of previous IPC strategies and co-design and implementation strategy with stakeholders(Y1-Y2). The project will conduct clinical and laboratory surveillance of HAI before implementing an IPC programme co-created with partners (Y2-4). Assessment of effectiveness of the implementation will be made and shared with policy makers (Y3-5 & WS4). Using mathematical modelling to understand the intervention (Workstrand 2): will recruit cohorts of patients with different types of HAI and study them in-depth by capturing comprehensive patient and bacterial data before and after implementation for key HAI syndromes (Y3-5). The project will use cutting edge microbiological tools and mathematical methods to analyse these data and iteratively improve the IPC programme. Health economics (Workstand 3): It will be vital to estimate the cost of HAI, and then evaluate cost effectiveness of interventions in order to enable policy makers to make recommendations about targeting efforts (Y2-4).Policy (Workstrand 4): We will actively involve MoH, KUHES and other key stakeholders throughout the project and, in doing so, co-create nationally scalable IPC interventions (Y4-5). Patient and public engagement will involve patents and the public in co-producing IPC strategy and interventions and in doing so raise the profile of HAI, IPC and AMR in Malawi, in partnership with MLW's community advisory group. Dissemination - The findings will be shared with the WHO Infection Prevention team and more broadly to the academic community through presentation and peer-reviewed publication. We will engage with the public through MLW's communications team, which uses radio, print and social media, and share information with the hospitals through peer education meetings (i.e. Grand Round), and with the Ministry of Health through relevant technical advisory groups
